claims.claim: Both IL10 ligand and receptor are conserved in vertebrates.
claims.source: Both ligand and receptor are conserved in vertebrates, and zebrafish has been discussed as a model for understanding IL10 biology (Piazzon et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation and general knowledge of vertebrate biology.

claims.claim: Chicken IL10 mRNA contains multiple copies of the AUUUA instability motif in the 3'-untranslated region.
claims.source: Like the mammalian transcript, chicken IL10 mRNA contains multiple copies of the AUUUA instability motif in the 3'-untranslated region.
claims.evidence: Based on sequence analysis and comparison with mammalian transcripts.

claims.claim: Quantitative variation in IL10 production may contribute to inter-individual or inter-breed variation in infectious disease susceptibility in chickens.
claims.source: We and others have provided evidence that quantitative variation in IL10 production may contribute to inter-individual or inter-breed variation in infectious disease susceptibility in chickens (Russell et al., 2021; Boulton et al., 2018a; Swaggerty et al., 2015; Calenge et al., 2009; Ghebremicael et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: The difference in spontaneous colitis phenotype between IL10-deficient chickens and mice may lie in the nature of the chicken intestinal microbiome.
claims.source: Since spontaneous colitis in mice depends upon resident enteric bacteria (Sellon et al., 1998), it is possible that the difference compared to the rodent models lies in the nature of the chicken intestinal microbiome (Bajagai et al., 2024), in which case the changes that we observed in the microbiome of IL10KO HOM chicks may serve to mitigate potential spontaneous intestinal pathology.
claims.evidence: Speculative reasoning based on cited mouse studies and observed microbiome differences.

claims.claim: Deletion of IL10 from the genome or selection in favour of low IL10 expression alleles need not necessarily affect production traits in chickens.
claims.source: In any case, the results indicate that deletion of IL10 from the genome or selection in favour of low IL10 expression alleles (Boulton et al., 2018a; Ghebremicael et al., 2008; Boulton et al., 2018b; Freem et al., 2019) need not necessarily affect production traits.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the absence of major growth or health effects in IL10-deficient chickens.

claims.claim: Findings with Campylobacter in IL10KO HOM birds are consistent with elevated intestinal inflammation in a broiler breed with relatively low IL10 expression.
claims.source: Findings with Campylobacter in IL10KO HOM birds are consistent with elevated intestinal inflammation in a broiler breed with relatively low IL10 expression, albeit a significant reduction in caecal colonisation relative to breeds with higher IL10 expression was not observed (Humphrey et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison with cited study on broiler breeds.

claims.claim: Variation in C. jejuni colonisation between timepoints, birds and repeated experiments is typical and has been reported when evaluating vaccines against C. jejuni colonisation.
claims.source: This is typical of C. jejuni colonisation in chickens, where bacterial population structures have been reported to be variable and unpredictable (Coward et al., 2008). Similar variation between time intervals, birds and repeated experiments has been reported when evaluating vaccines against C. jejuni colonisation (e.g. Buckley et al., 2010; Nothaft et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies documenting variability in C. jejuni colonisation.

claims.claim: In mammals, Salmonella has been reported to gain a competitive advantage from intestinal inflammation, both owing to availability of tetrathionate that Salmonella can uniquely use as a respiratory electron acceptor and remodelling of the indigenous microbiota.
claims.source: In mammals, Salmonella has been reported to gain a competitive advantage from intestinal inflammation, both owing to availability of tetrathionate that Salmonella can uniquely use as a respiratory electron acceptor (Winter et al., 2010) and remodelling of the indigenous microbiota (Rogers, 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Salmonella pathogenesis in mammals.

claims.claim: It is unclear if Salmonella derives the same benefits during colonisation of the avian intestine as it does in mammals.
claims.source: It is unclear if Salmonella derives the same benefits during colonisation of the avian intestine and the counts of viable bacteria recovered from the caeca of WT and IL10KO HOM birds can only be interpreted as the balance of bacterial growth and killing.
claims.evidence: Speculative statement about the applicability of mammalian findings to avian systems.

claims.claim: Coccidiosis has been estimated to exert costs in excess of £10 billion every year to the chicken production industry.
claims.source: Coccidiosis has been estimated to exert costs in excess of £10 billion every year to the chicken production industry (Blake et al., 2020), with E. tenella among the most common and pathogenic species (Clark et al., 2016; Long et al., 1976).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on the economic impact of coccidiosis.

claims.claim: Feeding antibody to IL10 receptor 2 (but not receptor 1) reduced lost BWG, but had no effect on oocyst shedding.
claims.source: Similarly, feeding antibody to IL10 receptor 2 (but not receptor 1) reduced lost BWG, but had no effect on oocyst shedding (Arendt et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to a study using anti-IL10 receptor antibodies.

claims.claim: Feeding chickens genetically modified corn expressing IL10 improved BWG and reduced oocyst shedding and caecal lesions.
claims.source: Feeding chickens genetically modified corn (Zea mays) expressing IL10 improved BWG and reduced oocyst shedding and caecal lesions (Lessard et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to a study using IL10-expressing corn.

claims.claim: The results from feeding studies with IL10-related interventions are consistent with the phenotypes associated with a reduction, rather than complete absence, of IL10 observed in the current study.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the phenotypes associated with a reduction, rather than complete absence, of IL10 observed here.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of cited feeding studies with the current experimental results.

claims.claim: IL10KO HOM birds or hypomorphs might be hyper-sensitive to more virulent bacterial infections and viral pathogens, such as avian influenza, that can elicit a cytokine storm.
claims.source: Given the excessive inflammatory activation we observed in non-lethal infections, and the literature in mice, IL10KO HOM birds or hypomorphs might be hyper-sensitive to more virulent bacterial infections and viral pathogens, such as avian influenza, that can elicit a cytokine storm.
claims.evidence: Speculative prediction based on observed inflammatory responses and mouse literature.

claims.claim: IL10KO HOM birds might be primed for a more rapid and effective response to more virulent infections.
claims.source: On the other hand, they may be primed for a more rapid and effective response.
claims.evidence: Speculative alternative prediction based on observed enhanced pathogen clearance.

claims.claim: The findings highlight the intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response.
claims.source: Our findings highlight the intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response and have important implications for the development of strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
claims.evidence: Summary statement based on the overall experimental findings showing trade-offs between pathogen clearance and pathology.

claims.claim: The findings have important implications for the development of strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
claims.source: Our findings highlight the intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response and have important implications for the development of strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the practical implications of the experimental findings.

results.result: Two IL10-deficient chicken lines were successfully generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology: IL10KO (complete knockout via premature stop codon) and IL10EnKO (enhancer deletion targeting a conserved regulatory region). Both lines produced viable offspring at Mendelian ratios.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 collectively demonstrate successful generation of IL10-deficient chicken lines using established CRISPR/PGC methodology. The molecular characterization (C2-C4) is supported by sequencing data and sequence conservation analysis, and Mendelian inheritance (C5) confirms germline transmission.

results.result: IL10KO HOM macrophages completely lack IL10 protein expression and show increased nitric oxide production. IL10KO HET macrophages show approximately 50% reduction in IL10 expression without dosage compensation, with intermediate effects on nitric oxide production.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are supported by ELISA and Griess assay data (Figure 2A-B) demonstrating complete loss in HOM, partial loss in HET, and functional consequences on nitric oxide production. The lack of dosage compensation (C9) is directly evidenced by the ~50% reduction in HET rather than maintenance of normal levels.

results.result: IL10-deficient chickens raised under SPF conditions do not develop spontaneous colitis or show significant growth defects, contrasting with the phenotype observed in IL10-deficient mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 are supported by longitudinal monitoring data, growth curves (Figure 3A-B), and histopathological scoring (Figure 3C) showing absence of spontaneous intestinal pathology. The contrast with mouse models (C14) is appropriately supported by citations and direct comparison of phenotypes.

results.result: IL10 deficiency significantly alters the caecal microbiome composition in chickens, with enrichment of Firmicutes and specific genera in IL10KO HOM birds, and clear separation of microbial communities based on beta diversity analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20 are supported by 16S rDNA sequencing data (Figure 4A-D), LEfSe analysis showing differential abundance of specific taxa, and PCA demonstrating significant community separation (R²=0.25, p=0.017). The conclusion that IL10 regulates microbiome composition (C20) is appropriately inferred from these data.

results.result: IL10KO HOM birds raised in conventional (non-SPF) facilities remained healthy with comparable growth rates to WT controls, though both genotypes showed significantly higher cellular infiltration scores in intestinal tissues compared to SPF-raised birds.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by growth curve data (Figure 3D) and histopathological scoring (Figure 3F). The increased cellular infiltration in conventional vs SPF environments (C23) is statistically significant and suggests environmental modulation of the IL10-deficient phenotype.

results.result: IL10KO HOM birds showed differential antibody responses to routine vaccinations, with significantly lower titres to AEV and IBDV, significantly higher titres to EDS and IBV, and no difference for CAV, ILTV, and NDV compared to WT controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 5) with appropriate statistical analysis. The vaccine-specific differences suggest IL10 deficiency affects adaptive immune responses in a context-dependent manner, though the biological significance and mechanisms remain unclear.

results.result: IL10KO HOM birds showed reduced C. jejuni colonization at early timepoints in two independent cohorts, associated with significantly increased inflammatory cell infiltration and elevated pro-inflammatory gene expression in the caecum.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 and C36 are supported by bacterial burden data (Figure 6A), histopathology (Figure 6 supplements 1-2), and gene expression analysis (Figure 6B). The variability between cohorts and timepoints (C27-C29) is acknowledged and consistent with known C. jejuni colonization patterns. The summary claim (C36) appropriately integrates findings across both bacterial challenges.

results.result: IL10KO HOM birds showed enhanced clearance of S. Typhimurium by 2 weeks post-infection compared to WT birds, associated with increased inflammatory cell infiltration and elevated pro-inflammatory gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by bacterial burden data (Figure 6C), histopathology (Figure 6 supplement 3), and gene expression analysis (Figure 6D). The temporal progression from marginal effects at 1 week to significant clearance at 2 weeks is clearly documented.

results.result: IL10KO HOM birds showed nearly complete ablation of E. tenella parasite replication with increased caecal lesions and reduced body weight gain, while IL10KO HET and IL10EnKO HOM/HET birds showed reduced lesions without affecting body weight gain.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 7A-B), histology (Figure 7C-D), lesion scores (Figure 7E-F), and body weight measurements (Figure 7G-H). The contrasting phenotypes between complete knockout and partial reduction of IL10 highlight a dose-dependent relationship between IL10 levels, pathogen clearance, and immunopathology.

results.result: Time-course analysis of E. tenella infection in IL10KO HOM birds confirmed accelerated pathogen clearance with reduced oocyst shedding, accelerated lesion development, sustained weight loss through day 8 with recovery by day 10, and peak inflammatory gene expression at day 6 coinciding with peak pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by comprehensive time-course data including parasite burden (Figure 8A), oocyst counts (Figure 8B), lesion scores (Figure 8C), body weight gain (Figure 8D), and gene expression (Figure 8E). The temporal coordination of these parameters provides strong evidence for the mechanistic relationship between IL10 deficiency, inflammation, and pathogen clearance.

results.result: IL10-deficient chickens do not develop spontaneous colitis but show enhanced pathogen clearance with increased inflammation in bacterial and parasitic challenge models. Complete IL10 knockout (but not heterozygous or enhancer mutations) results in effective pathogen elimination at the cost of increased immunopathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 appropriately summarize the major findings from all challenge experiments. The conclusions are well-supported by the combined data from bacterial (C. jejuni, S. Typhimurium) and parasitic (E. tenella) infections, demonstrating a consistent pattern of enhanced clearance with increased inflammation in IL10KO HOM birds.

results.result: Prior work in mammals has established IL10 as an essential regulator of intestinal inflammation, with IL10-deficient mice developing spontaneous enterocolitis dependent on the microbiome, and human IL10 mutations associated with inflammatory bowel disease. IL10 is conserved across vertebrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C59 accurately summarize prior work on IL10 biology in mammals, supported by appropriate citations to primary literature and reviews. These claims provide essential context for interpreting the chicken studies and are appropriately referenced.

results.result: Chicken IL10 mRNA contains AUUUA instability motifs similar to mammalian transcripts, and quantitative variation in IL10 production has been associated with infectious disease susceptibility in chickens.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by sequence analysis and multiple citations to prior studies. These claims establish the rationale for investigating IL10 function in chickens and provide context for the genetic approach.

results.result: The absence of spontaneous colitis in IL10-deficient chickens may be due to differences in the chicken intestinal microbiome compared to mice. IL10 deletion or selection for low IL10 expression need not necessarily affect production traits in chickens.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is speculative and appropriately qualified as such in the text. While the microbiome differences are documented (C15-C20), the causal relationship to absence of colitis is not directly tested. Claim C63 is inferred from the absence of major growth/health effects but is limited by the SPF/conventional housing conditions and may not generalize to commercial production environments with different pathogen exposures.

results.result: The findings with C. jejuni in IL10KO HOM birds are consistent with prior observations in broiler breeds with low IL10 expression. Variability in C. jejuni colonization between timepoints and experiments is typical and has been reported in vaccine studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 appropriately contextualize the C. jejuni results within prior literature. The acknowledgment of variability (C65) is important for interpreting the inconsistencies between cohorts and is well-supported by citations.

results.result: In mammals, Salmonella gains competitive advantage from intestinal inflammation through tetrathionate respiration and microbiota remodeling, but it is unclear if the same mechanisms operate in avian intestine.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 accurately summarizes mammalian literature with appropriate citations. Claim C67 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about applicability to avian systems, which is important for interpreting the enhanced Salmonella clearance observed in IL10KO HOM birds.

results.result: Prior studies targeting IL10 signaling during Eimeria infection showed variable effects on pathology and parasite burden. The current results are consistent with phenotypes associated with IL10 reduction rather than complete absence.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C70-C72 appropriately summarize prior intervention studies and contextualize the current findings. The comparison between complete knockout and partial reduction (C72) is well-supported by the differential phenotypes observed in IL10KO HOM vs HET/IL10EnKO birds.

results.result: IL10KO HOM birds might be hyper-sensitive to more virulent infections that elicit cytokine storms, or alternatively might be primed for more rapid and effective responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are explicitly speculative predictions about untested scenarios. While they are reasonable hypotheses based on the observed phenotypes and mouse literature, they represent future work rather than supported conclusions from the current study.

results.result: The findings highlight the intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response between pathogen elimination and immunopathology, with important implications for developing strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 appropriately synthesize the major findings demonstrating the trade-off between enhanced pathogen clearance and increased inflammation/pathology. The implications for poultry disease control strategies (C76) are reasonably inferred from the data, though specific applications would require additional development.

results.result: The authors generated two IL10-deficient chicken lines using CRISPR/Cas9: IL10KO (complete knockout via premature stop codon) and IL10EnKO (enhancer deletion targeting a conserved regulatory region). Both lines produced viable offspring at Mendelian ratios.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accepted the generation of the knockout models without criticism. Reviewer 1 noted 'the study is well executed' and Reviewer 2 stated 'CRISPR technology was employed to generate IL10 knock out chickens in both exon and putative enhancer regions.' The editor summarized 'Generating genetic knockouts, Meunier et al. established...' indicating acceptance of the methodology.

results.result: In vitro characterization of BMDMs showed complete absence of IL10 protein in IL10KO HOM cells with increased nitric oxide production, while IL10KO HET cells showed ~50% reduction in IL10 expression without dosage compensation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. Reviewer 1 stated the study 'first performed in vitro LPS stimulation based experiments' and the editor confirmed 'In vitro analysis of macrophage response to lipopolysaccharide confirmed the loss of IL10 protein expression, the lack of dosage compensation in heterozygotes, and prevention of autocrine inhibition of nitric oxide production.'

results.result: IL10-deficient chickens raised in both SPF and conventional facilities did not develop spontaneous colitis, maintained normal growth, and showed no overt intestinal pathology, contrasting with IL10-deficient mouse models.
results.evaluation: This finding was highlighted as a major result by all reviewers. The editor stated 'unlike mouse models, IL10 deficiency did not provoke spontaneous colitis in chickens.' Reviewer 1 noted 'At a steady-state level, however, IL-10 ablation did not lead to spontaneous colitis.' This species difference was treated as a key finding throughout the reviews.

results.result: IL10 deficiency significantly altered the caecal microbiome composition, with clear separation between IL10KO WT and HOM birds based on beta diversity analysis, showing enrichment of different bacterial phyla and genera.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the microbiome findings. Reviewer 2 stated 'IL-10 play an important role in the composition of the caecal microbiome' and the editor noted 'IL10-deficiency significantly altered the composition of the caecal microbiome.' The statistical significance (p=0.017) and clear separation in PCA were not questioned.

results.result: IL10KO HOM birds showed differential antibody responses to various vaccine antigens, with significantly lower titres to AEV and IBDV but higher titres to EDS and IBV compared to WT controls.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed in detail by reviewers, this finding was not challenged and fits within the overall acceptance of the immune characterization. The editor's statement that 'the strength of evidence is convincing' and Reviewer 1's comment that the study is 'well executed' implicitly support these data.

results.result: Following bacterial challenges with C. jejuni and S. Typhimurium, IL10KO HOM birds showed enhanced pathogen clearance associated with elevated pro-inflammatory gene expression and increased inflammatory cell infiltration, though with variable kinetics between experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly supported these findings. The editor stated 'a complete lack of IL10 strengthened immunity against enteric bacteria in chickens' and 'enhanced clearance of the pathogens was associated with elevated transcription of pro-inflammatory genes and increased infiltration of inflammatory cells.' Reviewer 1 noted the study demonstrated 'enhanced pathogen clearance' with 'enhanced inflammation related pathology and gene expression.'

results.result: E. tenella infection in IL10KO HOM chickens resulted in nearly complete ablation of parasite replication but was associated with significantly increased caecal lesions and reduced body weight gain, while IL10KO HET and IL10EnKO mutations showed reduced lesions without affecting parasite burden or weight gain.
results.evaluation: This trade-off was highlighted as a central finding by all reviewers. The editor stated 'pathogen clearance was accelerated but caecal lesions were more severe and weight gain was compromised.' Reviewer 1 noted 'complete ablation of IL10 leads to enhanced inflammation related pathology and gene expression, and enhanced pathogen clearance.' The dose-dependent effects were accepted without challenge.

results.result: Neither heterozygous IL10 knockout nor homozygous IL10 enhancer mutations had major effects on pathogen clearance or inflammation across the challenge models.
results.evaluation: This finding was implicitly accepted by reviewers as part of the overall dose-dependent effects. The editor's summary and reviewers' acceptance of the study's conclusions support this interpretation. No reviewer challenged the differential effects between genotypes.

results.result: The findings highlight an intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response with implications for developing strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the broader implications. The editor stated 'The observation may have implications for the livestock industry' and Reviewer 1 noted 'the applicability of this information in combating pathogen infection in livestock species in sustainable industries like poultry, the study is worth publishing.' The trade-off between pathogen clearance and tissue damage was recognized as significant.

results.result: The authors discuss potential mechanisms for species differences in spontaneous colitis, variability in bacterial colonization, and speculate about responses to more virulent pathogens, while noting that IL10 deletion need not affect production traits.
results.evaluation: These interpretive and speculative claims were not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 1 stated 'While the results are expected, and not surprising, this appears to be the first report to conclusively demonstrate IL-10's anti-inflammatory role upon its genetic ablation in avian model,' accepting the discussion of species differences. The speculative nature of some claims was appropriate for the Discussion section.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on IL10 protein loss and functional consequences (C6-C9). Both evaluations support the ELISA/Griess assay findings showing complete loss in HOM, partial loss in HET, lack of dosage compensation, and effects on nitric oxide production. OpenEval and peer reviewers both find evidence convincing.

Perfect agreement on microbiome findings (C15-C20). Both evaluations accept the 16S rDNA sequencing data, LEfSe analysis, PCA results (R²=0.25, p=0.017), and conclusion that IL10 regulates microbiome composition. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on vaccine response findings (C24-C26). Both evaluations support the ELISA data showing vaccine-specific differences in antibody responses. Peer review implicitly accepts these findings as part of overall immune characterization, while OpenEval notes biological significance remains unclear.

Perfect agreement on broader implications (C75-C76). Both evaluations affirm the trade-off between enhanced pathogen clearance and increased inflammation/pathology, and recognize implications for poultry disease control strategies. Reviewers explicitly noted applicability to livestock industry.

Strong agreement on knockout model generation (C1-C5 vs C2-C5). OpenEval includes C1 (overall methodology claim) while peer review focuses on C2-C5 (molecular characterization and inheritance). Both evaluations fully support the CRISPR/PGC methodology and germline transmission without criticism.

Strong agreement on absence of spontaneous colitis (C10-C14, C21-C23). OpenEval R3 addresses C10-C14 while peer R3 includes environmental effects C21-C23. Both highlight this as a major finding distinguishing chickens from mouse models. All reviewers treated this species difference as a key result.

Agreement on environmental modulation findings (C21-C23). OpenEval R5 specifically addresses growth and histopathology differences between SPF and conventional environments. Peer R3 groups these claims with the broader colitis findings (C10-C14), accepting environmental effects as part of the phenotypic characterization.

Strong agreement on bacterial challenge findings (C27-C31, C36 vs C27-C36, C49). OpenEval focuses on C. jejuni and summary claims, while peer review encompasses both bacterial pathogens. Both accept enhanced pathogen clearance with elevated inflammation and acknowledge variability between cohorts.

Agreement on Salmonella challenge findings (C32-C35). OpenEval R8 specifically addresses S. Typhimurium temporal progression. Peer R6 groups these with broader bacterial challenge results (C27-C36, C49), accepting the temporal dynamics from marginal effects at 1 week to significant clearance at 2 weeks.

Strong agreement on dose-dependent effects and trade-offs (C38-C42 vs C38-C42, C43-C47, C50). OpenEval R9 focuses on contrasting phenotypes between HOM and HET. Peer R7 encompasses both bacterial and parasitic challenges, highlighting the central finding of pathogen clearance vs tissue damage trade-off.

Agreement on Eimeria challenge findings (C43-C47). OpenEval R10 addresses parasitic infection time-course data. Peer R7 groups these with bacterial challenges (C38-C50), accepting the comprehensive evidence for enhanced clearance with increased inflammation across all pathogens tested.

Agreement on summary of bacterial challenge findings (C48-C51, with C49 overlap). OpenEval R11 summarizes all challenge experiments. Peer R6 addresses bacterial challenges specifically. Both accept the consistent pattern of enhanced clearance with increased inflammation, though peer review groups findings differently.

Agreement on overall challenge experiment conclusions (C48-C51, with C50 overlap). OpenEval R11 provides comprehensive summary across all pathogens. Peer R7 emphasizes dose-dependent effects and trade-offs. Both evaluations support the integrated findings from bacterial and parasitic infections.

Agreement on differential genotype effects (C48-C51, with C51 overlap). OpenEval R11 summarizes major findings including dose-dependent effects. Peer R8 implicitly accepts differential effects between genotypes as part of overall conclusions. Both support the pattern across all challenge experiments.

Agreement on speculative/interpretive claims (C62-C63 vs C62-C65, C67, C73-C74). OpenEval rates C62-C63 as UNCERTAIN due to speculative nature and lack of direct causal testing. Peer review accepts these interpretive claims as appropriate for Discussion section, not challenging the speculation about microbiome-colitis relationship or commercial applicability.

Agreement on C. jejuni contextualization (C64-C65). OpenEval supports these claims as appropriate literature context. Peer R10 groups with other interpretive claims, accepting the acknowledgment of variability and species differences without challenge.

Agreement on mammalian literature context (C66-C67). OpenEval supports C66-C67 as appropriate contextualization with acknowledgment of uncertainty about avian applicability. Peer R10 accepts discussion of species differences, noting this is the first conclusive demonstration in avian models.

Agreement on intervention study context (C68, C70-C72). OpenEval supports these claims as appropriate summary of prior work and comparison between complete knockout and partial reduction. Peer R10 implicitly accepts this contextualization as part of overall discussion framework.

Agreement on speculative predictions (C73-C74). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting these are speculative predictions about untested scenarios representing future work. Peer R10 accepts these as appropriate speculative claims for Discussion section without challenge.

OpenEval R12 addresses background claims on mammalian IL10 biology (C52-C59). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. These literature context claims were not explicitly discussed by peer reviewers, though they form the foundation for interpreting the chicken studies.

OpenEval R13 addresses chicken IL10 sequence conservation and rationale (C60-C61). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. Peer reviewers did not explicitly comment on these foundational claims establishing the basis for investigating IL10 function in chickens.
